Those two facts fit together, but not in the way a relaxed credit constraint would predict: a farm applying less of an input sits farther up its own response curve, so a higher marginal product is what one expects of a group that uses less fertilizer, not evidence that finance has loosened the fertilizer margin. The Ethiopian evidence therefore stands as a contrast to what these data show rather than a confirmation of it, and the contrast is one more reason to ask, as Section 5.4 does, whether the borrowing recorded here is the kind that finances fertilizer at all.

Two readings of the land result are consistent with the data, and the design cannot separate them. One is that credit-using households are operating where area is the binding factor, so that additional land still adds substantially to output; an elasticity describes the curvature of a group’s frontier at its mean input bundle, and a high land elasticity is what a frontier looks like at a point where the complementary inputs are thin — which, as Figure 1 shows below, is exactly where these farms sit, applying less of every purchased input per hectare than their matched comparators. The other is compositional: the group frontier is fitted on the borrowing households as they are, and a frontier fitted on a group that differs in farm size, tenure or agro-ecology can display a higher land elasticity without any change in how a given household farms. The returns-to-scale contrast sharpens the question rather than settling it. Credit users’ frontier shows mildly increasing returns (1.049) where non-users’ shows slightly decreasing ones (0.971), so a proportional expansion of all inputs would raise output more than proportionately for the borrowing group — which is what an unrelieved liquidity constraint looks like from the production side, and which sits pointedly beside the finding of Section 5.3 that the same group operates farther from best practice. Table S3 adds one feature worth carrying forward to the heterogeneity results, and it is a reversal rather than a difference of degree. The coefficient on the cocoa area share is negative in the naive national frontier (-0.117) and more strongly negative in the non-user frontier (-0.216), but positive and large in the credit-user frontier (0.553), all significant at the 1% level. Under the technology non-users operate, a larger cocoa share is associated with lower output at given inputs; under the technology credit users operate, with higher output. The credit-user technology is therefore favorable to cocoa in a way the comparison group’s is not, even though, as shown below, it is less favorable to every other crop.

The last two columns of Table 4 give the meta frontier elasticities on the matched and unmatched samples. The two are close and preserve the same ranking of inputs: land is 0.699 matched against 0.713 unmatched, family labor 0.166 against 0.169, planting material 0.035 against 0.038, pesticide 0.020 against 0.018, and returns to scale 0.959 against 0.971, with hired labor and fertilizer coinciding to within a thousandth. Balancing the sample therefore changes the shape of the envelope only modestly; its main effect, shown next, is on the position of the two groups relative to it. What the elasticities establish is that the best-practice technology, like both group technologies, is land-intensive with near-constant returns to scale, so the technology gaps discussed next are gaps in the level of the frontier rather than in its shape.

5.3 Technology gaps, technical efficiency and meta-frontier efficiency

Table 4 decomposes performance into the technology gap ratio of Equation (4), pure technical efficiency from Equation (2) and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency, from Equation (5); the Matched rows are the preferred estimates and the Unmatched rows show what balancing the sample changes.

The technology gap is the headline result, and it runs against H1. In the matched sample the mean TGR is 0.926 for non-users and 0.822 for credit users: the technology set operated by non-users produces, on average, 93% of the output attainable under the best-practice technology at the same inputs, and that of credit users 82%. The difference of 10.4 percentage points is significant at the 1% level, is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5, and is negative. Section 4.1 hypothesized the opposite on the grounds that credit finances the lumpy investments that move a farm toward best practice. In these data borrowing households are not, as a group, operating the best-practice technology; their frontier lies farther inside the meta frontier than the frontier of comparable non-users, and matching on gender, round, region, agro-ecology, locality and a rich set of household, farm and financial-inclusion covariates does not remove that difference. The unmatched gap is of the same sign and similar size (8.8 percentage points), so the finding is not created by matching either.

Pure technical efficiency, which measures each group against its own frontier, differs little between the groups. On the matched sample mean TE is 0.596 for non-users and 0.612 for credit users, a difference of 1.7 percentage points in favor of credit users that is significant at the 1% level and is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5. What is unstable is not the sign within the matched sample but what happens when the samples are not balanced: unmatched, the same comparison runs 2.7 percentage points against credit users, and Section 5.5 shows that the sign also moves across the definition of who borrowed and across aggregation rules. Both differences are statistically significant, because the jackknife standard errors are small; but a difference that reverses when the comparison group is rebalanced, and that stays within a few percentage points of zero under every specification examined, is not one on which an interpretation should rest. The defensible statement is that, relative to their own technology, credit users and matched non-users are about equally efficient, each attaining roughly 60% of their own frontier output, a level of within-technology inefficiency in line with earlier Ghanaian frontier studies [12], [14], [15]. H2, which predicted lower efficiency among credit users, is not supported: in the balanced comparison the small difference runs the other way, and we do not read these data as establishing an efficiency effect of borrowing in either direction.

Because the efficiency margin is close to neutral, the meta-frontier efficiency gap is the technology gap. Matched MTE is 0.554 for non-users and 0.508 for credit users, a statistically significant shortfall of 4.6 percentage points, reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5. The MTE gap is negative, significant and of the same order as the TGR gap, so the shortfall of credit-using households relative to best practice is a technology gap and not an efficiency gap. Both groups, it should be stressed, operate well inside the meta frontier, at about 55% and 51% of attainable output; the credit gap is a modest increment on a large common shortfall of the kind widely documented for African smallholders [6], [12], and the economically relevant statement is not that borrowers farm worse but that the technology they farm with is, on average, farther from the best available, by an amount several times the efficiency difference in either direction. The attribution differs from the one [12] report across agro-ecologies, where technical inefficiency outweighs technology differences. The two results are not in conflict, because they decompose different contrasts, but together they caution against assuming that any production shortfall in Ghana is a management problem.

The comparison between the matched and unmatched rows of Table 4 shows what matching does to these contrasts, and it is the most informative feature of the table. In the unmatched sample credit users trail non-users by 2.7 percentage points in TE and 7.7 points in MTE, several times the matched values, whereas the unmatched TGR gap is close to the matched one. Balancing the two groups on observables therefore removes almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and most of the raw MTE deficit, but leaves the technology gap essentially intact. The raw efficiency deficit was compositional, a statement about who borrows on the dimensions Section 4.3 balances; the technology gap survives the comparison of like with like. Observable selection into borrowing explains the efficiency difference and almost none of the technology difference.

Figure 1 sets the frontier results beside the input and output levels of the matched pairs. For each of the six frontier inputs, expressed per hectare, and for the real value of output per hectare, we estimate the proportional gap associated with credit as a log-linear treatment effect on the matched pairs, for the matched sample as a whole and separately over the covariate distributions of non-users and of users, with the same jackknife inference as the frontier estimates. These gaps are the input-intensity counterpart of the frontier comparison: the frontiers say how much output a group’s technology yields from a given bundle, and Figure 1 says whether credit users in fact apply a different bundle, so that a contrast arising because borrowers operate a different technology can be distinguished from one arising because they use more or less of the same inputs.

Credit-using households apply substantially less planting material, hired labor, pesticide and fertilizer per hectare than their matched comparators, the planting-material gap being by some way the largest and each of the four significant at the 1% level; land area, against which the other inputs are normalized, registers no gap; household labor does not differ significantly; and the value of output per hectare is slightly higher for credit users, a difference that does not approach conventional significance. The three reference populations give nearly identical gaps, so the pattern does not depend on which group’s covariate distribution is used. Two things follow. First, the hired-labor advantage of borrowing households in the unmatched data of Table 1 (33 against 24 man-days per hectare) does not survive comparison with observably similar non-borrowers; it reflected who borrows rather than what borrowing finances. Second, credit is not associated with intensification on the purchased-input margin in these data, which is the opposite of what a liquidity-relaxing account of credit predicts, and the input on which borrowers fall furthest behind is planting material rather than fertilizer, so the shortfall is not confined to the input for which seasonal finance is most often advocated. Read with Table 4, the picture is coherent: a borrowing group whose technology leans heavily on land and thinly on everything bought, whose household labor is neither more plentiful nor more productive at the margin, which lies inside the best-practice envelope, produces about as much per hectare as the comparison group, and is run about as efficiently, relative to that technology, as the comparison group runs its own. The lower TGR of credit users therefore cannot be read as borrowed money buying inputs that fail to raise output; it is the technology in use, evaluated at common input levels, that sits farther from best practice.

5.4 Interpreting the negative technology gap

The technology gap is measured against a meta frontier that envelops both group frontiers, so a lower TGR for credit users says that the technology of borrowing households, as a group, is not the best practice in the sample. It does not say what makes it so. Four readings are consistent with the evidence of Sections 2, 3 and 5.3, and the data discriminate among them only partially.

The first is loan use. Household credit relaxes the household’s liquidity constraint, not the farm’s, and the loan-purpose codes of Table 3 show that agriculture is a minority use of it: in 2012/13, the round in which the recorded purposes exhaust the loans, only 26.8% were taken for agricultural purposes, the remainder financing business, education, ceremonies, debt repayment and other household needs. Fungibility of agricultural credit within the household is well documented [24], and Figure 1 is what fungibility looks like on the farm: borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs. On this reading the negative technology gap is not a failure of credit to reach the farm so much as evidence that, for most of these households, the loan was never directed there, and the household indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. This is the reading the exhibits most directly support, and Table 5 adds to it the sharpest evidence the design can offer. Splitting the treatment by who in the household held the loan, the technology gap is indistinguishable from zero when the operator borrowed on their own account and widest when the spouse did (Table 5; Section 5.5 reports all four definitions). If the gap were a property of borrowing households as such, it should not vanish in the one case where the borrower and the farmer are the same person; that it does is what a loan-use account predicts, since the operator’s own loan is the one with the shortest path to the farm. The reading is also consistent with the northern-Ghana finding that even input-linked credit raised input use without proportionate output gains [19]. It remains a reading rather than a result: the survey records the stated purpose of a loan but not the use of each cedi, the operator-only estimate is imprecise as well as small.

The second is selection on what the GLSS does not record. Matching balances the covariates in Table 1 and Figure S1, but not the reasons a household applies for a loan and a lender grants it. Distress borrowing after a shock, borrowing to fund a non-farm enterprise, and lender targeting of households with particular repayment prospects would each place borrowers on a different technology for reasons the design cannot see, and allocation increasingly runs through community institutions the GLSS does not observe (Section 4.4). Differences in risk preference that affect both borrowing and technology choice belong here too [11]. The stability of the TGR gap between the unmatched and matched samples is consistent with this reading, since it shows that the gap is orthogonal to the observables the matching uses; it cannot show whether the gap is orthogonal to what the matching does not use, and the direction of the resulting bias is not signed. The pattern across borrowers in Table 5 sits awkwardly with a purely selective account, however. Selection on unrecorded farm circumstances should if anything be sharpest where the operator is the borrower, since that is the case in which the decision to borrow is most closely tied to the farm; instead it is the case in which no technology gap appears. That does not rule the reading out – who within a household borrows is itself a choice, and the operator-only estimate is imprecise – but a selection story has to explain why the gap is absent exactly where the selection into borrowing should be most farm-specific.

The third is the distinction between use and access. The treatment is an indicator of having borrowed, and the modal reason for not applying is having no need for a loan (56.2% and 61.7% of non-applicants in the two rounds, Table 3), so the comparison group mixes households that are credit constrained with a larger number that, on their own account, are not. The literature that finds credit constraints lowering farm productivity identifies the constrained explicitly [9], [10]; the contrast estimated here is a different object, and a negative gap for borrowers against a largely unconstrained comparison group is not in tension with it. If the households that choose not to borrow are, on average, the ones already operating the better technology, the estimated gap partly reflects that sorting. Table 6 offers a partial check. Within households in which the operator applied for a loan, a subgroup in which demand is held constant, the TGR contrast between credit users and applicants whose household did not obtain credit is -11.3 percentage points, close to the full-sample gap, so the headline gap is not an artefact of comparing applicants with non-applicants; the efficiency contrast in that row is considerably larger than in the full sample and the meta-frontier contrast correspondingly smaller, but the unfunded comparison group is small and is selected by lenders’ decisions, so we do not lean on either. Experimental evidence from Ghana approaches the same distinction from the supply side. Offering maize farmers in the north rainfall-index insurance and cash grants in varying combinations, [18] find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of the risk constraint and changed little when capital alone was supplied, which places the binding constraint for that population in uninsured risk rather than in liquidity. On that evidence a negative technology gap among borrowers is not in itself surprising, because relaxing a credit constraint need not move a farm’s technology when risk is what binds, and the near-absence of cover against production risk documented in Section 3 is part of the environment in which the loans observed here were taken. The experiment does not, however, settle the reading of the contrast estimated here: it supplied capital to farmers who did not have to seek it, in one crop and one region, so it speaks to access where this treatment records use, and it identifies which constraint binds where this design can only describe the households in which borrowing is observed.

The fourth is measurement. Section 4.3 argues that self-reported borrowing under-records small and informal loans, which would place some genuine borrowers in the comparison group and attenuate the contrast toward zero. Attenuation does not generate a negative gap; it makes the estimated gap, if anything, an understatement of the true difference in absolute value. It cannot explain the sign.

What the data cannot do is assign weights to these readings. The GLSS records the purpose of a loan but not what the household did with the liquidity it freed, records that a loan was granted but not why, and records use rather than access. The disaggregations of Section 5.6 narrow the space somewhat, because the technology gap is present in every financial-service subgroup and in nine of the ten regions, the exception being the least agricultural of them, which is difficult to reconcile with a story confined to one lending channel or one agro-ecology. The honest summary is that the negative technology gap is a robust description of Ghanaian borrowing households, not an estimate of what credit does to a farm.

Placed against the Ghanaian literature, the result reconciles rather than contradicts. Positive credit-efficiency associations have been reported for maize producers under program and input-linked financing [20], [22], modest output effects of input credit [19], and financial inclusion more broadly has been linked to smallholder productivity [23]. Those studies observe credit tied to farm inputs, or crops and regions in which such credit predominates, and they compare borrowers and non-borrowers on a single frontier; the estimates here are national in scope, net of matching on observables, and drawn from a population in which little household borrowing is agricultural. The nationally representative decomposition therefore does not show that agricultural credit fails to move farms toward the frontier; it shows that credit as households actually obtain and use it is not associated with best-practice technology and does not raise or lower within-technology efficiency in any robust way. The distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper’s substantive contribution to that literature.

Table S4 adds covariate detail that points the same way. In the matched meta frontier, whose one-sided term is the technology gap, the gap is larger for female-operated farms (coefficient 0.876) and smaller where the household owns its land (-0.368), uses mechanized equipment (-0.667), receives extension advice (-0.180) or grows a more diversified crop mix (-1.331), all significant at the 1% level, while years of schooling carries a small positive coefficient (0.028), meaning a larger distance from best practice. Distance from best practice is thus associated with the same tenure, service and gender factors that structure technology access in Ghanaian agriculture generally [14], [15], not with the borrowing indicator that defines the groups.

The policy reading follows from which channel carries the gap. A shortfall located in technical efficiency would call for managerial support through extension, training and record-keeping bundled with the loan; the evidence does not support that diagnosis, because the efficiency difference is small, of unstable sign, and disappears once borrowers are compared with similar non-borrowers. A shortfall located in the technology gap calls for changing the technology farms can obtain and use, but here the gap is not the technology gap that input-constrained farms display, because credit users apply fewer purchased inputs rather than more, and it appears alongside loans that are mostly not used on the farm. The finding therefore does not support expanding household credit as such as an instrument for closing Ghana’s crop technology gap, and it does not support the opposite proposition either, since the design cannot establish what credit does to a given farm. It is consistent with the view, long argued for agricultural finance in sub-Saharan Africa, that finance moves technology only when it is designed around the farm’s investment and timing needs and bundled with the inputs, information and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking [32], and with demand-side accounts in which low uptake reflects the limited value farmers see in the products on offer [25]. The bundling argument is consistent with these findings, but it is not tested by them; Section 6 draws out the implications after the robustness and heterogeneity evidence has been presented.

5.5 Robustness of the main findings

Three features of the main result need to survive scrutiny: the sign and size of the TGR gap, the smallness of the TE gap, and the consequent attribution of the MTE gap to technology. Efficiency scores are not specification-free. The inputs entered, the functional form, the distribution assumed for the one-sided term and the estimator used to recover producer-level scores can each move mean efficiency and the ranking of producers within the same data [49], so no single specification can establish the size, and still less the sign, of a difference between two groups’ scores; the spread of estimates across defensible specifications is itself the evidence, and we read it that way rather than selecting the specification that gives the cleanest answer. We examine each of the three features across the definition of treatment, the matched sample and the frontier specification, and the exercise separates them rather than confirming them together: the technology component holds its sign throughout and its size across everything except the identity of the borrower, while the efficiency component holds neither.

Table 5 varies whose borrowing defines the household as a credit user; each definition is fitted as its own pair of frontiers, so the non-user column varies across rows. The technology gap is negative and significant under three of the four definitions and indistinguishable from zero under the fourth, and the pattern of which is which is informative rather than merely reassuring. It is 10.4 percentage points under the household definition, 32.8 points when the spouse holds the loan and 6.6 points when another member does, each significant at the 1% level; but under the operator’s own credit it is 0.2 points and does not reach conventional significance. The technology gap, in other words, is absent precisely where the borrower and the farmer are the same person, and widest where the loan is held by the spouse. That ordering is difficult to reconcile with any account in which borrowing itself places a household on a poorer technology, and it is what the loan-use reading of Section 5.4 would predict: a loan taken by the operator is the one most likely to reach the farm, and it is the one associated with no technology gap at all. The efficiency component is significant under only two of the four definitions. It is 1.7 percentage points in credit users’ favor under the household definition and a much larger 20.6 points in their favor under spousal credit; under the operator-only and other-member definitions it is small and does not reach conventional significance, so no efficiency contrast is established there in either direction. The MTE gap, by contrast, is negative and significant under all four, from 3.0 points under the operator-only definition to 5.6 points under spousal credit. Overall performance relative to best practice is therefore lower for credit users however the loan-holder is defined, even under the one definition for which neither component reaches significance on its own. Two qualifications belong with this. The narrower definitions rest on far fewer treated observations than the household definition, so their standard errors are correspondingly larger and the operator-only null is an imprecise null rather than a demonstrated zero. And the matched sample is balanced on having household credit, not on who within the household holds it, so these rows compare differently composed borrower groups against differently composed comparison groups rather than isolating the identity of the borrower.

Figure S1 reports covariate balance for the unmatched sample and for each of the eight matched samples described in Section 4.3, on absolute standardized mean differences, variance ratios and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The unmatched sample is most imbalanced on schooling, household size and several crop-share, ethnicity and regional indicators. Every matched sample brings the standardized differences and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics close to zero on nearly all covariates, the propensity-score and robust Mahalanobis schemes bring the variance ratios closest to one, and the differences among the propensity-score schemes are small, so the choice among them is not consequential for balance; the probit propensity-score sample, which the composite ranking selects, underlies Tables 4 to 6 and Figures 1 to 4. Two covariates deserve mention. Household size is the one covariate on which a standardized difference of moderate size survives in every matched sample, and the propensity-score matches leave a moderate difference in operator age that the distance-based matches remove, so balance on those dimensions is imperfect; given the family-labor result of Section 5.2, this is a further reason not to over-read the small TE gap.

Figure S2 re-estimates the three gaps under the alternative specifications listed in Section 4.5, with the preferred estimate marked as a reference band. Across the eight matched samples, formed on Euclidean, scaled Euclidean, Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance and on logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit propensity scores, the TGR gap is negative and of similar size in every case, the MTE gap is negative in every case, and the TE gap is positive in every case, ranging from near zero to about two percentage points. The unmatched sample is the single point at which the efficiency gap changes sign: there it is negative and several times larger in magnitude, alongside a larger negative MTE gap and a TGR gap slightly closer to zero than the matched ones. The sign of the efficiency gap is therefore a property of whether the comparison group is balanced rather than of the estimator, which is the lesson of Table 4 restated across eight matching schemes. Computing scores by the Jondrow-type or the conditional-model estimator rather than the Battese-Coelli estimator, and aggregating operator-level scores by the simple mean or the median rather than the weighted mean, leave all three gaps close to the preferred estimate, and none changes sign. Replacing the Translog with a Cobb-Douglas frontier leaves the TGR and MTE gaps negative, but the Cobb-Douglas technology gap carries a standard error large enough that it is not distinguishable from zero, so the functional form matters for the precision of that estimate even where it barely moves its location. Lifting the regularity restrictions leaves the TGR gap unchanged to four decimal places and moves only the efficiency margins, the TE gap falling close to zero and the MTE gap becoming somewhat more negative. That the technology component is invariant to the regularity restrictions is a further reason to treat it as the robust finding and the efficiency margin as the fragile one.

The distributional assumption on the one-sided term is where the exercise reaches its limit, and the limit is worth stating plainly rather than summarizing away. The frontier is estimated under five distributions for the inefficiency term: the half-normal baseline, the exponential, the truncated skewed Laplace, the generalized exponential and the truncated normal. Three of the five agree closely. The half-normal, exponential and truncated skewed Laplace each give a negative technology gap – the latter two somewhat larger than the baseline – with usable jackknife standard errors, together with a small positive efficiency gap and a negative meta-frontier gap. The generalized exponential also gives a negative technology gap, but with a standard error several times the estimate, and it returns a positive meta-frontier gap; nothing can be read from it in either direction. The truncated normal does not estimate at all: it returns a positive technology-gap point estimate with no standard error, and no efficiency or meta-frontier estimate. We draw no inference from those two, and they mark the boundary of the claim rather than a qualification of it. The half-normal is retained as the baseline because it is the specification that estimates on every subsample and every jackknife replicate. The finding that credit users sit farther below the meta frontier is therefore established under three of the five distributions examined, and under every treatment-definition apart from the operator-only case, every functional form, efficiency estimator, aggregation rule, matching scheme and regularity variant; it is not established across all five distributions, and the paper does not claim that it is. Taken together, the robustness exercise ranks the three findings by their stability: the negative technology gap is the most robust, surviving every dimension except the identity of the borrower and the two distributions that fail to estimate; the negative MTE gap is robust in sign and moderately sensitive in magnitude; and the TE gap is small wherever it estimates, positive in every matched sample and negative only without matching, so its sign is a statement about the comparison group rather than about borrowing.

5.6 Heterogeneity across financial-service use, farmers, crops and regions

The gaps reported so far average over households that differ in their other financial services, their characteristics, their crops and their locations. This subsection asks where the technology gap and the efficiency gap are concentrated. The disaggregated estimates summarize the operator-level TGR, TE and MTE from the single matched meta frontier within each subgroup; the frontiers are not re-estimated by subgroup, so the estimates describe heterogeneity within the main result rather than separate models. In Table 6 each cell is the credit-user mean less the non-user mean within the stated group.

Figure 2 and Table 6 examine the contrast across financial-service use, which is where the paper’s framing in terms of financial inclusion rather than credit alone is tested. The technology gap is negative and significant within every financial-service subgroup the GLSS allows: -10.8 percentage points among households with a formal account, -11.1 among the insured, and, across institution types, from -5.4 points among the small group holding an investment or mortgage account to -15.4 among cooperative and credit-union members, with bank customers, savings-and-loans participants, susu members and mobile-money users falling between them. There is no financial-service configuration in these data within which borrowing households operate the best-practice technology, and holding another financial product does not narrow the technology gap of credit users.

What the disaggregation does not show is any complementarity between credit and formal account ownership. Figure 2 splits the contrast by whether the household holds a formal account, and the two halves are close to identical: the technology gap is marginally wider among account holders, the efficiency contrast is positive and of essentially the same size in both, and the resulting meta-frontier gaps differ by well under a percentage point. Account ownership neither amplifies nor offsets the credit contrast on either margin. Because the financial-inclusion literature anticipates that credit works better where it sits alongside savings and payment services [1], [23], the absence of any interaction is worth reporting in its own right; it is a null result rather than a reversal, and we report it as one.

Institution type is the one dimension on which the efficiency margin varies appreciably, and it does not resolve into a mechanism. The TE contrast runs in credit users’ favor in every institution type but one, from 1.1 points among customers of commercial, community and rural banks and 3.3 among mobile-money users to 4.2 in the investment or mortgage group, 4.7 among cooperative and credit-union members and 5.3 among susu-scheme participants; only among savings-and-loans participants does it run against them (-2.7 points). In the investment or mortgage group the advantage is large enough that credit users outperform matched non-users against the meta frontier by 1.6 points. The MTE gap is widest among savings-and-loans participants (-8.0 points) and customers of commercial, community and rural banks (-5.3). We do not read a mechanism into this ordering. The efficiency advantage is largest in the two group-based channels, susu schemes and cooperatives or credit unions, yet their meta-frontier gaps differ by more than two percentage points because their technology gaps do, which no account of peer monitoring or savings discipline predicts, and the subgroups are small and overlapping, since a household may hold several of these products at once. The data cannot say whether these patterns reflect the kind of credit each channel supplies, the kind of household that uses it, or the uses to which the liquidity is put. A decomposition of the credit contrast by the source of the loan and by its reported purpose, the two dimensions Table 3 records and that no current exhibit crosses with the operator-level scores, would test that directly; it is not available here, and we identify it as the cut the evidence most needs rather than anticipate what it would show. The source-of-information block of Table 6 is reported for completeness and not interpreted, because its category labels do not map consistently onto the corresponding block of Table 2 read in Section 3, and the reasons-for-no-account block, whose category indicators rest on the same response-coding mechanism, is likewise left uninterpreted.

Figure 3 disaggregates by operator gender, age and education. The technology gap is negative and significant in every group, so no demographic group of credit users operates a technology closer to best practice than its matched non-users. The gap is wider for female than for male operators, which is consistent with the larger technology gap for female-operated farms in Table S4 and with the gender gaps in technology use documented on the same data [14]; it narrows with operator age; and it is not monotone in schooling, being narrowest for operators with no formal education and wider at every level above it. The efficiency contrast favors credit users in most groups – more so for women than for men, and diminishing with age until it is indistinguishable from zero among operators aged sixty and over – but it runs against them in two: operators with junior secondary schooling and, more strongly, the small group educated beyond senior secondary level, for whom credit users are markedly less efficient within their own technology. The MTE gap is negative in every group, narrowest for operators with senior secondary schooling and with no formal education, where the efficiency advantage offsets part of the technology gap, and widest by a considerable margin for the post-secondary group, where the two margins compound. The expectation that better-educated, prime-age male operators would convert credit into technology gains more readily is not borne out; the technology gap is broad-based, and where the credit contrast is least adverse it is because of an efficiency offset rather than a narrower technology gap.

Figure 4 disaggregates by major crop and by administrative region. Across crops the technology gap is negative and significant for nine of the ten crops shown, widest for yam, cassava and maize and narrowest for sorghum and plantain; for cocoa alone it is indistinguishable from zero. There is thus no crop in which credit-using households operate a technology closer to best practice than their matched non-users, and the cocoa case is an absence of difference rather than an advantage. That absence remains consistent with the large cocoa-share coefficient in the credit-user frontier noted in Section 5.2, and cocoa is the one export crop, with sector-specific input and extension arrangements of its own [38]; whether it reflects those arrangements or the selection of better-endowed households into cocoa borrowing cannot be established from the survey, which does not record loan purpose by crop. The efficiency contrast is more uniform than it was across the other disaggregations: it favors credit users in every crop, significantly in nine of the ten and negligibly for sorghum. The MTE gap is accordingly negative for every crop except cocoa, widest for millet, groundnut and rice, and close to zero for plantain, where the efficiency advantage is largest and offsets most of a moderate technology gap. Across regions the technology gap is negative and significant in nine of the ten, widest in Volta, Brong Ahafo and Eastern and narrowest in Western and Northern; it is positive in Greater Accra, the only region in which credit users operate a technology closer to best practice and much the least agricultural region in the sample, so that estimate should not be read as a rural finding. The efficiency contrast favors credit users in eight regions, is indistinguishable from zero in Upper East and runs against them only in Western, and the MTE gap is negative in every region except Greater Accra, widest in the two Upper regions. The crop and regional patterns do not sort by agro-ecology or by cash-crop status, since the widest and among the narrowest technology gaps are both in southern regions, and they do not line up with the density of financial services in Table 2, so we do not attempt to attribute them. What they establish is that the technology gap is pervasive rather than concentrated in a few crops or locations, while the efficiency contrast, where it is not zero, runs mildly in credit users’ favor – a combination more consistent with readings that operate through the household, such as loan use and selection, than with one that operates through the lending environment.

For targeting, the heterogeneity results cut two ways. Because the technology gap is negative in nearly every subgroup, there is no identifiable class of borrowers, defined by service use, gender, age, schooling, crop or region, for whom credit use is associated with a technology closer to best practice; cocoa producers and, on the efficiency margin, cooperative and credit-union members are the nearest to exceptions. Where the subgroups differ is in whether credit users make up part of the technology gap through better within-technology performance, as unbanked households, younger and female operators, susu-scheme participants and plantain and groundnut producers do, or compound it, as banked households and the most educated operators do. That is a statement about where managerial support would and would not find a deficit to close, and about the fact that the subgroups in which the overall shortfall is largest, account holders and the post-secondary educated, are not those a financial-inclusion program would ordinarily prioritize; it is not evidence that credit itself works better for some groups than for others.

6. Conclusion

This paper asked whether the credit that Ghanaian crop-farming households obtain is associated with operating a better production technology, with using a given technology more efficiently, or with neither, and whether the answer depends on who in the household borrows, on the other financial services the household uses, and on the operator, the crop and the region. The question matters because the two margins call for different policy responses, and because the case for extending finance to smallholders rests on the first of them: credit is expected to relax the liquidity constraint that keeps farms from adopting best-practice technology. We addressed it with the farmer-level records of the two most recent rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, a household-level indicator of credit use rebuilt from the original questionnaires, group-specific stochastic frontiers enveloped by a stochastic meta frontier and estimated on a sample in which each credit-using household is paired with an observably similar non-user, and inference from a jackknife that re-runs matching and estimation in every replicate. Credit use is rare in this population, at 11.9% of operators, and the descriptive record of Section 3 showed that the loans behind that figure are mostly informal or group-based, mostly unsecured, mostly not for farming where their purpose can be observed, and obtained in an environment in which the modal non-borrower reports no need for a loan.

The answers to the three questions are consistent with one another and run against the hypothesis that motivated the analysis. First, credit-using and non-using households do operate different technologies, but the difference is not the one a liquidity-constraint story predicts: the group frontiers differ overwhelmingly in one input, the response of output to land, which is substantially higher for credit users and accounts for essentially the whole difference in returns to scale, while the responses to family and hired labor are marginally lower for them and those to fertilizer and pesticide marginally higher; and matched credit users apply less planting material, hired labor, pesticide and fertilizer per hectare than their comparators – planting material by the widest margin – while producing about as much. A technology that leans on land and thinly on purchased inputs, and that exhibits mildly increasing returns where the comparison group’s exhibits slightly decreasing ones, is not the technology of a household whose farm liquidity constraint has been relaxed. Second, the performance shortfall of credit users relative to best practice is a technology gap, not an efficiency gap. In the matched sample the technology gap ratio of credit-using households is 0.822 against 0.926 for their matched non-users, a shortfall of 10.4 percentage points: the technology set operated by borrowing households lies farther inside the best-practice frontier, not nearer to it. Technical efficiency within each group’s own technology differs by an amount that is small and not stable in sign – it favors credit users in the balanced comparison and runs against them before balancing – and meta-frontier efficiency is correspondingly lower for credit users, by 4.6 percentage points. Balancing the two groups on observables removed almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and little of the technology gap, which locates the credit-associated shortfall in the frontier borrowing households operate rather than in how they manage it. Third, the technology gap is pervasive across settings but not across borrowers. It holds under every matching scheme, functional form, efficiency estimator, aggregation rule and distributional assumption estimated, and within every financial-service subgroup, every gender, age and education group, nine of the ten regions and nine of the ten major crops; the exceptions are cocoa, where credit users are at no technological disadvantage, and Greater Accra, much the least agricultural region in the sample. Where it does not hold is in who borrowed. Splitting the treatment by which household member held the loan, the gap is widest for spousal credit, intermediate for other members, and indistinguishable from zero when the operator borrowed on their own account – an ordering that a story about borrowing households as such does not predict, and that points instead to how far the loan sits from the farm. The efficiency contrast varies in sign from one setting to another and is most adverse for the most educated operators; it does not, however, vary with formal account ownership, which neither widens nor narrows the credit contrast on either margin, so the complementarity between credit and other financial services that the inclusion literature anticipates does not appear in these data.

These are findings; what follows is interpretation, and the design bounds it. The estimates are associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample. Four readings of the negative technology gap are consistent with the evidence. The one the exhibits most directly support is that household credit in this population mostly does not finance the farm: fewer than one in three loans were taken for agricultural purposes in the round in which purpose can be observed, credit is fungible within the household, and borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs, so the indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. The others are selection into borrowing on characteristics the survey does not record, the pooling of unconstrained non-borrowers with constrained ones in the comparison group, and the attenuation that misreported informal loans would produce, which cannot explain the sign. The data cannot rank these readings, and none of them implies that extending credit would lower the technology a given farm operates. What the results rule out is the account in which household credit, as farm households in Ghana actually obtained it between 2012/13 and 2016/17, is associated with movement toward the best-practice technology. They do not show that agricultural credit fails to raise farm technology, because the credit observed here is for the most part not agricultural credit; the distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper’s substantive contribution to a Ghanaian literature that has so far studied credit tied to particular crops, schemes and regions against a single frontier.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions, and they are specific rather than generic. The estimation sample is a complete-case sample formed at two stacked points: the harmonized financial module retains operators aged eighteen or more with recorded age, schooling, account and insurance status, and the financial-inclusion index that enters the matching distance is built on complete cases of the same indicators; the matching then requires complete information on every matching covariate. Neither restriction is guaranteed to be random with respect to financial-service use, so the matched contrast describes the completely observed population of credit users and their nearest comparators rather than the population of Ghanaian crop farmers. The index itself is a summary rather than a measurement, and Note S1 now sets out what it does and does not capture: it is the first principal component of fourteen indicators of schooling, financial-sector employment, insurance holding and account ownership, fitted within survey-round and locality strata and min-max scaled over the pooled sample, and the component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in that indicator set, roughly twice the fourteenth an uninformative component would take, so it is informative but far from dominant. Its content is also not identical across the two rounds: travel insurance has too little variation to enter the component in either 2016/17 stratum, so thirteen indicators rather than fourteen underlie the index there, and the account-ownership item recognizes mobile-money accounts only in that round. A different indicator set or scaling would therefore change which non-user is paired with which user, and although the estimates are stable across eight matching schemes, their sensitivity to the index specification has not been examined directly, and nothing here should be read as an effect of inclusion as an index. The indicator records credit use rather than access, so the contrast is between borrowers and non-borrowers rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained. Matching cannot balance managerial ability, risk preference, land quality, wealth outside the surveyed modules or standing with the group-based lenders that supplied a rising share of loans, the survey offers no credible instrument, and the design assumes that lending to one household does not change the terms available to its neighbors, an assumption that group lending intermediated through the same communities makes uncomfortable. Finally, the data are repeated cross-sections in which credit use and production are observed in the same survey interview, so the estimates cannot separate credit that finances this season’s technology from credit that follows a bad one, and they say nothing about the trajectory of a farm’s technology after a loan.

Within these limits the implications for policy are clear about direction if not about mechanism. Expanding the volume of household credit as such should not be expected to close the technology gap in Ghanaian crop production, because the households that borrow are not, on this evidence, the ones operating the best-practice technology, and their loans are not observable as an intensification of the farm. The shortfall is not managerial, so extension and training aimed at how borrowers use their inputs would not find the deficit they were designed to close. The evidence instead points to the conditions under which credit becomes farm investment: loan products sized and timed for crop production, bundled with the input supply, advisory services and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking, in a setting where distance and collateral requirements have already fallen while the share of farmers reporting no need for a loan rose from 56.2% to 61.7%. The variables the estimates associate with proximity to the best-practice technology, extension contact, mechanization and secure tenure, are those a technology-oriented policy would act on, and cocoa, the one crop with sector-specific input and extension arrangements, is the one crop in which credit users are not at a technological disadvantage. Whether these associations reflect what such arrangements do, or who selects into them, is exactly what the present design cannot say.

Three lines of research would resolve what this study cannot. Panel data on the same households, or a source of variation in credit access unrelated to farm performance of the kind that experimental relaxations of credit and risk constraints have supplied for Ghanaian farm households [18], would separate the technology in use before borrowing from the technology after it and would distinguish credit that finances investment from credit that follows a shock. Survey modules that link the purpose and source of each loan to the plot on which inputs are applied, and that elicit credit-constraint status directly rather than borrowing alone, would allow the loan-use and use-versus-access readings to be tested rather than argued from aggregate purpose shares. And a decomposition of the credit contrast by loan source, which the estimation objects already carry but no exhibit reports, would show whether the technology gap is a feature of relational and group-based borrowing in particular or of household borrowing in general. Until such evidence exists, the appropriate reading of these results is that financial inclusion in Ghana has broadened on the savings and payments margin faster than on the credit margin, that the credit farm households do obtain is not associated with better production technology, and that the policy problem is less the supply of loans than the design of products that farm households would borrow for and invest on the farm. For a financial-inclusion agenda that expects credit to carry farms toward the frontier, the question this raises is not how to lend more but what the loans that farm households already take are buying.

Appendix

Note S1. Financial-Inclusion Index Construction

The financial-inclusion index introduced in Section 4.3 summarizes the non-credit dimensions of a farm household member’s engagement with financial services. It is built on one record per household member, with that member’s demographic characteristics averaged over the plots the member works, merged by enumeration area, household and member identifier to the harmonized financial-services release from which the indicators of Table S0 are drawn. The index is the first principal component of 14 indicators: the member’s years of schooling, whether the member works in a financial institution, whether another member of the household does, whether the member owns an account with a financial institution or contributes to a savings scheme, and ten indicators of insurance cover (vehicle, medical, funeral, property, commercial, travel, life, retirement, education and other endowment or investment plans). The component is fitted on complete cases across all 14 indicators; on the current release the financial indicators are themselves complete, so that restriction binds only through years of schooling, which is carried down from the farmer file. Composite measures of this kind are standard in work that treats financial inclusion as a multidimensional construct spanning accounts, savings and insurance rather than as account ownership alone, in Africa as elsewhere [1], [3].

Three indicators available in the same release were deliberately left out: the community distances to the nearest bank, motorable road and public transport (Table S0). Coverage is the first reason. The community questionnaire is administered per enumeration area and does not reach every area, so the three distances are missing for about a fifth of the members in the release, and the complete-case rule would drop every one of them. That loss is not random. It falls disproportionately on urban enumeration areas in 2012/13, which is precisely the imbalance the harmonization avoids by joining the community block to the farmer records rather than restricting to it, so admitting the distances here would reintroduce the same selection one stage later. Construct is the second reason. The distances describe a place rather than a person and enter with the sign opposite to every other indicator, so a component that included them would mix how financially connected a member is with how far that member lives from a bank. Excluding them makes the index unambiguously the former and removes the need to reason about sign when the loadings are read.

Because the two rounds differ in the services they record and rural and urban localities differ in the services available, a component is fitted separately within each survey-round-by-locality stratum rather than once over the pooled data: on 8,083 members in rural GLSS6, 1,527 in urban GLSS6, 5,692 in rural GLSS7 and 971 in urban GLSS7, against 16,273 in the pooled fit that supplies the reference metric. The sign and the scale of a principal component are arbitrary, so the four stratum scores are not comparable as estimated. Each is therefore placed on the pooled component’s metric by regressing the pooled score on the stratum score within the stratum and retaining the fitted values, a rescaling that fixes orientation as well as scale: where a stratum’s component came out sign-flipped, the regression coefficient is negative and the fitted values still align with the pooled score. The strata are disjoint, so the rescaled scores coalesce into a single value for every member. Three variables are released. FinIdx is the rescaled component itself. FinIdxSi is FinIdx min-max scaled over the pooled sample to the unit interval, and it is the variable that enters the matching distance of Section 4.3. FinIdxCat is the weighted quintiles of FinIdx, also taken over the pooled sample. Both transformations are pooled rather than within-round, so they express a member’s absolute position on the index and not a rank within a survey round; and because the scaling is min-max, FinIdxSi is by construction sensitive to a single extreme value, which compresses the remaining members into a narrower band than a rank or quantile transform would.

Table S6 reports the first-component loadings and the share of variance the component explains in each stratum, and they warrant a careful reading rather than a reassuring one. In the pooled fit every loading is positive and the two largest are on years of schooling and on account ownership, followed by life and vehicle insurance and by financial-sector employment, so the pooled metric is oriented in the direction the index’s name implies and the rescaling carries that orientation into every stratum. Two departures qualify this. Travel insurance has no variation in either 2016/17 stratum and is screened out of both, so the index rests on 14 indicators in 2012/13 and on 13 in 2016/17; taken with the fact that account ownership captures mobile money only in the later round, the index’s content is not identical across the two rounds. And one loading is negative: commercial insurance in the urban 2016/17 stratum. It is near enough to zero to carry little weight in the score, but a mixed sign pattern is the signal that a first component is picking up something other than inclusion, and it is reported here rather than smoothed over. The more consequential diagnostic is the explained variance. The first component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in a set of 14 indicators, where a component carrying no information at all would account for about a fourteenth. The component is therefore informative but far from dominant: the indicators it summarizes are only loosely correlated with one another, a single dimension does not come close to exhausting them, and a different indicator set or a different scaling would produce a different ordering of members. This is the substantiation of the limitation that Section 6 states, and it is the reason the index is used to balance a comparison rather than to carry an interpretation.

What the index is not, finally, is the treatment. The treatment throughout this paper is credit_hh, the household credit indicator defined in Section 2.2 and documented in Table S0. The index enters in two other roles: FinIdxSi is one covariate in the distance on which each credit-using household is paired with a non-user, so that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services (Section 4.3), and FinIdxCat is available in the estimation as a dimension of heterogeneity. No exhibit in this paper reports results by the index’s quintiles; heterogeneity across financial services is examined on the observed indicators themselves, formal account ownership above all (Figure 2 and Table 6). The index is estimated on 16,273 household-member records, a larger set than the 15,696 farm operators of the analysis sample, so index values exist for records the frontier analysis does not use; the matching draws on the values it needs and discards the rest.

The table states the specification rather than any estimate. Frontier, shifter and inefficiency rows are the arguments passed in 004_MSF_financial_inclusion_study.R; matching rows are the covariate lists of 002_MATCHING_financial_inclusion_study.R. The corresponding estimates are in Tables 4, S3 and S4.

Expected signs are the a priori expectations of Section 4.1, not findings. An em dash marks a variable for which the paper posits no expectation; "Not applicable" marks a variable that enters an exact-match stratum or a matching distance rather than a regression, so that no coefficient sign exists to expect. The criterion for the matching covariates is balance between users and non-users, reported for each of them in Figure S1.

The inefficiency covariates scale the variance of the one-sided error term, so a positive coefficient means greater inefficiency and, in Equation (3), a larger technology gap; a negative expected sign therefore means the variable is expected to place the farm closer to its frontier. 004_MSF passes the same vector as inefficiency_covariates and as adoption_covariates, so each row in that block governs both margins.

Positive signs on the six inputs follow from monotonicity of the production function and are not a prediction about credit. H3 of Section 4.1 is a prediction about a difference of elasticities between groups -- credit users' frontier more responsive to land and labor, and not more responsive to fertilizer -- which no single row can carry.

004_MSF passes the survey round as a factor in both the frontier shifters and the inefficiency determinants, but Tables S3 and S4 print no round coefficient; see the note to those tables.

The treatment, credit_hh, is not listed because it is a regressor in none of the three specifications: it partitions the sample into the groups whose frontiers are compared (Section 4.2) and supplies the flag on which pairs are drawn (Section 4.3). It is documented in Table S0. Pairing further requires complete information on the identifiers, the survey weight and the treatment flag, and an observation missing any matching field is dropped before pairs are formed.

Data source: Ghana Living Standards Survey [waves 6-7].

Entries are loadings on the first principal component, estimated over the pooled sample and separately within each survey-round-by-locality stratum by 000_INDEX_financial_inclusion_study.do. GLSS6 is the 2012/13 round and GLSS7 the 2016/17 round.

Rows are ordered by the pooled loading, largest first. An em dash marks an indicator that does not enter a stratum's component: it has no variation in that stratum and is screened out before estimation, so the loading is absent rather than zero, as with travel insurance. The component rests on 14 indicators in 2012/13 and 13 in 2016/17, so its content is not identical across the two rounds.

Loadings are as estimated within each stratum, before the stratum scores are placed on the pooled component's metric. The sign and scale of a principal component are arbitrary, so a sign pattern is informative within a column and not across columns; in the pooled fit every loading is positive, so a higher index score means greater financial inclusion, and the rescaling carries that orientation into every stratum (Note S1).

The share of variance explained is the proportion of the total variance of the indicator set carried by the first component. With 14 indicators, a component carrying no more than an equal share would account for about 0.071.

Observations are household-member records. The index is estimated on more records than the analysis sample of farm operators uses; the matching draws the values it needs (Note S1).

Data source: Ghana Living Standards Survey [waves 6-7].
